title: Dorton v. Collins & Aikman Corp.
summary: “Subject to” the seller’s terms did not clearly make acceptance conditional on the buyer’s assent; arbitration’s inclusion required further findings.
notes:
Court: Sixth Circuit (1972).

Important remand questions: Was there an oral contract? Was arbitration already a term? If newly proposed, did it materially alter the bargain? Compare C. Itoh’s explicitly conditional language and Bayway’s discussion of a different jurisdiction’s arbitration rule.

sections.Parties: The Carpet Mart partners sued Collins & Aikman, their carpet supplier, for alleged fraud and misrepresentation about fiber quality.
sections.Material Facts: The parties made about fifty-five transactions over three years. The buyer ordered by telephone; the seller sent acknowledgments containing arbitration on the reverse. The forms used “subject to” language and purported to make retaining the form or accepting delivery sufficient. The buyer received and paid for carpets without objecting.
sections.Procedural History: After removal on diversity grounds, the district court denied a stay pending arbitration, using § 2-207(3) to exclude the clause. The Sixth Circuit remanded for further factual findings under the correct formation and term-selection analysis.
sections.Issue: Did the forms prevent formation under § 2-207(1), and, if not, was arbitration already agreed or added through § 2-207(2)?
sections.Holding: The forms did not clearly condition acceptance on the buyer’s assent in the statutory sense. Whether arbitration became a term required findings about the prior oral transactions and material alteration.
sections.Reasoning: The proviso requires a clear indication that the offeree will not proceed without assurance of assent to the additional or different terms. “Subject to” and a list of conduct or inaction purportedly sufficient to bind the buyer did not meet that standard. An acknowledgment could be an acceptance or a confirmation of an already completed oral contract. Arbitration might even have been part of the oral bargain. If it was an additional term, both parties’ merchant status brought § 2-207(2) into play, and materiality required facts. The opinion does not categorically hold all arbitration clauses immaterial or all material.
